subject: sociology
title: Crime & Subcultures: Evaluation & Modern Subcultures
welcome_lead: Subcultural theory critiqued — and revived by post-modern street style.
meta_desc: A-Level Sociology crime subcultures evaluation post-modern Maffesoli neo-tribes.
final_note: Subcultures persist but look more like tribes than gangs.

concepts.def: Online groups with deviant or oppositional identity.
Hayward & Young — emotional driver of consumer-era crime.

walkthroughs.body_html: Classic theories (Cohen, Cloward & Ohlin, Miller) assume shared values, focus on boys, and treat crime as collective. McRobbie & Garber (1976): girls were ignored — bedroom culture. Modern girls' street activities visible in Batchelor (2009) Glasgow study.

Maffesoli (1996): neo-tribes — fluid, fashion-led, multiple memberships. Muggleton (2000): post-subculturalists pick and mix styles. Cultural criminology (Hayward 2002) sees crime as emotional kick in a status-anxious consumer society.

Murray (1990): an underclass defined by welfare dependency, family breakdown and crime. Critics (Walker, Lister): blames the poor for structural inequality. UK 2010s 'broken Britain' rhetoric uses similar logic. Left realism blames relative deprivation, not culture.
